subject: religious-studies
topicDisplay: New Testament Studies Study Of A World Religion
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The concept of ijtihad in Islamic jurisprudence refers to:
options: Blind imitation of past scholars
Independent reasoning to derive legal rulings
The consensus of the whole Muslim community
The recitation of the Qur'an from memory
questions.explain: Ijtihad is the disciplined exercise of independent juristic reasoning, contrasted with taqlid (uncritical following), and is central to debates about Islam in the modern world.

questions.q: Calvin's 'sensus divinitatis' refers to:
options: A proof of God derived from cosmic motion
An innate awareness or sense of the divine implanted in all people
The sixth sacrament of the church
The hierarchy of angels in heaven
questions.explain: Calvin's sensus divinitatis is the inborn sense or awareness of God he believed exists in every human being.

questions.q: For Augustine, the highest human good and the goal of the will is:
options: Political stability in the earthly city
The acquisition of earthly wisdom
The summum bonum, the love and enjoyment of God
Freedom from all bodily desire
questions.explain: For Augustine the summum bonum is God, whom the rightly ordered will loves and enjoys above all else.

questions.q: Compared with Orthodox Judaism, Reform Judaism is generally characterised by:
options: A belief that the Torah was not divinely inspired at all
Rejection of all ethical teaching of the Torah
A more liberal stance, treating much halakhah as non-binding and historically conditioned
Stricter adherence to the totality of halakhah
questions.explain: Reform Judaism emphasises ethical monotheism and individual autonomy, regarding ritual law as evolving and not uniformly obligatory, in contrast to Orthodoxy's binding halakhah.

questions.q: The doctrine of 'limited election' (limited atonement) holds that:
options: Salvation depends entirely on human free choice
Everyone will ultimately be saved regardless of faith
Christ's saving work is effective only for the elect chosen by God
God elects new people in every generation by lottery
questions.explain: Limited election teaches that Christ's atonement is intended and effective only for a particular elect group.

questions.q: Which biblical narrative does Augustine treat as the origin of original sin?
options: The Fall of Adam and Eve in Genesis 3
The Exodus from Egypt
The Flood and Noah's ark
The Tower of Babel
questions.explain: Augustine grounded original sin in the disobedience of Adam and Eve recounted in Genesis 3.

questions.q: In the theology of religions, 'exclusivism' is the view that:
options: Salvation is found only through explicit faith in Christ
All religions lead equally to salvation
Non-Christians are saved by sincere following of their own faith
God's existence cannot be known at all
questions.explain: Exclusivism holds that salvation comes only through explicit faith in Jesus Christ.

questions.q: Bonhoeffer's notion of 'costly grace' is contrasted with:
options: Predestination
Works righteousness alone
Cheap grace, which offers forgiveness without discipleship or repentance
Natural law ethics
questions.explain: Bonhoeffer opposed 'costly grace', which demands discipleship, to 'cheap grace', which claims forgiveness without commitment or repentance.

questions.q: Rosemary Radford Ruether, unlike Daly, generally argued that:
options: Patriarchy is divinely ordained
Christianity is wholly irredeemable for women
Christianity can be reformed and contains liberating resources for women
Feminism and theology are incompatible
questions.explain: Ruether sought to reform Christianity from within, holding it contains liberating resources, whereas Daly ultimately rejected it.

questions.q: For Bonhoeffer, true discipleship requires:
options: Strict separation of faith from the world
Comfortable acceptance of grace without obedience
Concrete obedience and willingness to follow Christ even at great cost
Avoidance of all suffering
questions.explain: Bonhoeffer taught that genuine discipleship means costly, concrete obedience to Christ, even to the point of suffering.

questions.q: The concept of the 'imago Dei' teaches that human beings are:
options: Wholly identical in nature to God
Created in the image and likeness of God
Merely advanced animals with no spiritual nature
Reincarnated divine spirits
questions.explain: The imago Dei is the doctrine that humans are made in the image of God, grounding their dignity and capacity for relationship with him.

questions.q: For Christians who treat the Bible as the supreme moral authority, ethical decisions should ultimately be grounded in:
options: The traditions of secular philosophy
The teaching of scripture as God's revealed word
The unaided conscience alone
Majority public opinion
questions.explain: A Bible-centred ethic locates final moral authority in scripture understood as God's revelation.

questions.q: John Hick's pluralism employs which famous analogy to describe the religions?
options: The watch and the watchmaker
The cave and its shadows
Different paths up the same mountain, with God as the common ultimate reality
A potter shaping clay
questions.explain: Hick's pluralism likens the religions to different culturally conditioned responses to one ultimate divine Reality.

questions.q: Understanding Jesus as 'liberator' stresses that he:
options: Avoided all conflict with political authorities
Endorsed the existing social hierarchy without question
Sought purely individual, inward salvation only
Challenged oppression and proclaimed freedom for the marginalised and poor
questions.explain: The liberator model highlights Jesus' challenge to injustice and his concern for the poor and oppressed.

questions.q: Augustine used the term 'concupiscence' primarily to describe:
options: The rational ordering of the will toward God
Disordered desire that resists the rule of reason and will
The divine grace that heals fallen nature
The original harmony of Adam before the Fall
questions.explain: Concupiscence is Augustine's term for the disordered, uncontrollable desire afflicting fallen human nature.

questions.q: The Christian claim that God is 'omnibenevolent' is most directly challenged by which theological problem?
options: The problem of the historical Jesus
The problem of evil and suffering
The problem of religious language
The problem of the Eucharist's nature
questions.explain: An all-loving, all-powerful God appears in tension with the existence of gratuitous evil, the central problem addressed by theodicies such as Augustine's and Irenaeus's.

questions.q: The phrase 'already but not yet' is used in New Testament scholarship to describe the Kingdom of God as:
options: Inaugurated in Jesus' ministry but awaiting full consummation
Entirely future and absent from the present
Already completed at Jesus' birth
A purely human ideal with no divine action
questions.explain: The 'already but not yet' captures the Kingdom as begun in Jesus yet not fully realised until the end.

questions.q: 'Universalism' regarding salvation is the view that:
options: Hell is eternal for the majority of humanity
Ultimately all people will be reconciled to God and saved
Only a fixed number of the elect will be saved
Salvation is impossible without church membership
questions.explain: Universalism is the belief that God's salvation will eventually embrace all people.

questions.q: Liberation theology, associated with figures such as Gustavo Gutiérrez, is best characterised by its emphasis on:
options: Withdrawal from political engagement
The primacy of monastic contemplation
A 'preferential option for the poor' and structural justice
Literal biblical inerrancy
questions.explain: Liberation theology reads the Gospel as a call to confront social and economic oppression, prioritising the liberation of the marginalised.

questions.q: In Sikhism, regarding the Guru Granth Sahib as the 'living Guru' means that:
options: It replaces belief in one God
A human Guru continues to be appointed in each generation
Only the Ten Gurus may interpret it
The scripture itself holds the eternal authority of Guruship after Guru Gobind Singh
questions.explain: Guru Gobind Singh declared the scripture the eternal Guru, so the Guru Granth Sahib carries living spiritual authority and is treated with the reverence due a Guru.

questions.q: The Bhagavad Gita's teaching of karma yoga primarily advocates:
options: Ritual sacrifice as the sole path to the divine
Withdrawal into silent meditation alone
Performing one's duty without attachment to the fruits of action
Renouncing all action to attain liberation
questions.explain: Krishna instructs Arjuna to act in accordance with his dharma while relinquishing attachment to outcomes, presenting selfless action as a path to liberation.

questions.q: Among the six orthodox darshanas of Hindu philosophy, the Samkhya school is distinctive for its:
options: Strict monotheism centred on Vishnu
Rejection of the concept of liberation
Denial of the authority of the Vedas
Dualism of purusha (consciousness) and prakriti (matter)
questions.explain: Samkhya posits a fundamental dualism between pure consciousness (purusha) and primal matter (prakriti), and liberation comes through discriminating between the two.

questions.q: For Calvin, the natural human knowledge of God is rendered ineffective for salvation because:
options: Reason has no role whatsoever in religion
God has hidden himself entirely from creation
Human sin distorts and suppresses the sensus divinitatis
Nature contains no evidence of a designer
questions.explain: Calvin argued that sin corrupts and suppresses the innate sense of God, so saving knowledge requires grace and revelation.

questions.q: The Three Marks of Existence (tilakkhana) in Buddhism are:
options: Anicca, dukkha and anatta
Greed, hatred and delusion
Birth, ageing and death
Body, speech and mind
questions.explain: The three marks are impermanence (anicca), unsatisfactoriness/suffering (dukkha) and not-self (anatta), characterising all conditioned phenomena.

questions.q: A key doctrinal emphasis distinguishing Mahayana from Theravada Buddhism is:
options: Rejection of the Buddha's authority
The abolition of monastic life
The bodhisattva ideal of compassionate postponement of nirvana for all beings
The denial of karma
questions.explain: Mahayana elevates the bodhisattva who vows to liberate all sentient beings, alongside concepts such as sunyata, whereas Theravada emphasises the arhat's individual liberation.

questions.q: The Khalsa, established by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699, is best described as:
options: A monastic order requiring celibacy
The community of initiated Sikhs committed to the discipline and the Five Ks
A council that elects future Gurus
A purely ceremonial title with no obligations
questions.explain: The Khalsa is the order of committed, initiated (amritdhari) Sikhs who uphold a code of conduct (rahit) including the Five Ks, blending spiritual devotion with moral discipline.

questions.q: The principal theological distinction underlying the Sunni–Shia division concerns:
options: Whether God is one or many
Whether the Qur'an is created or uncreated
The direction faced during prayer
The legitimate succession of authority after Muhammad
questions.explain: Shia Islam holds that leadership rightly passed to Ali and the Imams of the Prophet's household, whereas Sunnis accept the caliphate, a dispute over rightful authority.

questions.q: In Sikh teaching, the practice of sewa (selfless service) and langar (the communal kitchen) chiefly express:
options: The earning of merit to escape rebirth alone
A requirement only for the Gurus
Equality of all people and devotion expressed through service
Ritual purity laws separating communities
questions.explain: Langar and sewa embody the Sikh rejection of caste and social hierarchy, enacting human equality and devotion to God through humble service to others.

questions.q: In the New Testament, the 'Kingdom of God' proclaimed by Jesus is best understood as:
options: A literal earthly political state founded by Jesus
God's reign or rule, both present and yet to come
An exclusively post-mortem heaven only
A description of the Roman Empire
questions.explain: The Kingdom of God refers to God's sovereign rule, present in Jesus' ministry yet awaiting future fulfilment.

questions.q: Within the Noble Eightfold Path, 'Right Mindfulness' (samma sati) belongs to which of the three traditional divisions?
options: Dana (generosity)
Sila (ethical conduct)
Samadhi (mental discipline/meditation)
Panna (wisdom)
questions.explain: The Eightfold Path is grouped into wisdom, ethics and meditation; mindfulness and concentration fall under samadhi, the cultivation of disciplined mental states.
